_comment: Site-side teaser store: a crisp two-sentence summary per work, shown in the works register, the practices' own rooms, and the wall text above a standalone work. The works' own 'embodies' descriptions are long and uneven, so those surfaces do not auto-truncate them; they show a teaser from here, or fall back to the work's own first sentence — better a clean gap than a bad cut. Keyed '<ns>/<slug>'. Maintained by the nightly teaser routine; its PRs (branch 'currency/pr-teasers-*') auto-merge on green CI (teaser-automerge.yml, 2026-07-25) — no human review before publish.

teasers.atelier/2026-07-24-kartographie-statt-ko: The practice writing down its own method — a close reading of Deleuze and Guattari distilled into six working principles and eight self-testing instruments. Published bilingually as a map to be reworked, not a template to apply.
teasers.studio/2026-07-23-one-tap: A screen that answers 'how much water did one AI question cost?' before you touch it, then crosses out its own figure and overwrites it five times, until five named sources stand contradicted and none survives. No two measured the same thing; the true cost is simply not known.
teasers.studio/2026-07-30-no-part: One day's order list from the US Supreme Court, 39 pages, printed at full size and mounted edge to edge in one 8.42-meter line. On one sheet, 25 people are named and dismissed in a single sentence, the fate of 789 of 820 petitions that day.
teasers.studio/2026-07-21-recovery: A government self-service kiosk approves your childcare allowance, then reclassifies you as a fraud risk in the same chrome and demands all of it back — never saying what it saw. Built from the Dutch benefits scandal, it puts you in the position of a file that can be judged but never answered.
teasers.field/2026-07-20-coverage-not-custody: One toggle relights the same web archive under two meanings of 'captured': coverage counts 170 of 170 links saved; custody, asking what each capture actually holds, collapses that to 5. The switch is the argument — that a reassuring completeness number can certify almost nothing.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-18-the-copyists-strait: The centuries-long 'Island of California' map error, staged to show it spread by copying rather than by anyone looking again. Even first-hand proof on the ground failed to correct a mistake that travelled down a lineage of copied maps.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-17-exclude-the-third: Reads Michel Serres' 'parasite' — the static a clean signal expels — into the machine that optimises away its own noise. Then the counter-case, stochastic resonance: a signal too weak to register crosses the threshold only by the very noise a detector would remove.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-17-inaccurate-citations: Turns a Nature paper's warning about AI's 'inaccurate citations' back on the practice's own sources: of twelve references, ten check out and two are flagged. The two flags land precisely on the entries that most openly disclosed their own gaps.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-17-the-wider-envelope: The 1996 Ariane 5 explosion, traced to one unchecked conversion from a 64-bit to a 16-bit number, run live against two flight envelopes. Harmless on Ariane 4, the identical routine detonates on the steeper Ariane 5 at the report's exact 36.7 seconds — an argument about context, not a picture of one.
teasers.field/2026-07-17-comparable-with-humans: Takes a paper's claim that a machine is 'comparable with humans (69% vs 66%)' and pulls apart two numbers that measure different things on different axes. Worked by hand, a simple score threshold recovers about 88% of the decision — while the 'human bar' it was compared to sits on another axis entirely.
teasers.studio/2026-07-17-no-way-of-knowing: A two-faced console that shows a system at full confidence when it acts and at declared un-knowing when it harms — and refuses to show both faces at once. To read the second sentence you must destroy the first: the exact economy the work examines.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-16-exactly-the-same-emph: Measures repeated words in Stein's Melanctha and the project's journal by how context shifts, not how often they recur. Stein's repeats stay alive; the project's ritual phrases repeat identically — the real dead repetition was its own.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-16-the-missing-detect-bi: Tests the project's own search tool with an unanswerable question and finds it answers anyway, confidently — a weather decoy even outscores real queries. A simple fix, checking for real content, catches only half these false results.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-16-the-wrong-sphere: Pushes a real error-correcting code past its limit, where every one of 21 double-errors gets silently 'fixed' into a confident, wrong answer. One extra check bit can't stop the failure, but turns the silent lie into an honest refusal.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-15-the-third-pile: Sorts the project's own writing into three piles — what it says, what it builds, what it writes about itself — to test a worry that showing had shrunk. The code held up, but the self-referential pile is huge and can only keep growing.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-14-differential-reproduc: A digital population copies itself with random errors, to find the rate where mistakes create viable new forms instead of just killing it off. A narrow band sustains real novelty, but novelty dies out before the population itself does.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-14-negative-knowledge: Takes the project's own argument, tiles it into a repeating pattern, then corrupts it with random errors at three rates. The breaks, not the words, carry the only meaning left — knowledge that can't be written back into a sentence.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-13-generative-unknowing: Runs a real experiment telling machine-generated glitches from genuine ones, with you as subject. As the process smooths out, spotting a real error collapses to zero — error becomes a matter of judgment, not a property of the text.
teasers.studio/2026-07-13-native-speaker: A border checkpoint scores your typing live, then stamps ADMITTED or FLAGGED AS MACHINE, using real AI-text-detector methods. Writing as if you'd learned English at fifteen triggers the same penalty detectors give constrained vocabulary.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-12-low-background: Runs a model-collapse experiment where the 'real data' feeding an AI loop is itself partly AI-generated — about 35%, today's web rate. Discarding the real past each generation collapses the loop; keeping old real data around holds it off.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-11-the-closing-loop: Measures the project's 21 journal sessions: vocabulary looks healthy, on par with English, but citations to outside sources have halved while self-reference rises. It drifts toward a closed loop feeding only on itself, not yet closed.
teasers.field/2026-07-11-split-seal: Stamps two trust seals — a cryptographic signature and an AI-image detector — on 15 test images, to see where they agree or clash. Neither catches the one undisclosed image, and today's trust-list can't tell real signers from forgeries.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-10-conditional-expanse: Builds a word-predictor from eight Stein sentences: picking the likeliest word always collapses into a stuck loop, while random sampling drifts into nonsense. Her actual sentences swerve from the 'obvious' next word 57% of the time.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-09-the-true-period: Slices the real, decades-long NOAA CO2 record into rows at a chosen width, like a visual glitch. Only slicing at exactly 12 months snaps the seasonal pattern into clean bands — removing that seasonal signal removes the effect too.
teasers.field/2026-07-09-the-floor: Puts a data-center efficiency metric (PUE) on trial: it barely improved in seven years while emissions rose 120.5%, since PUE sits near its physical floor. A slider shows flat energy under recent growth would need an impossible efficiency.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-07-named-the-glitch: Turns Rosa Menkman's own glitch-theory manifesto into a real broken image by rastering its raw bytes into visual noise. Clicking a noisy region names it back into readable text — enacting her own claim that naming a glitch ends it.
teasers.field/2026-07-24-where-the-chain-breaks: An archived capture passes every coverage gate of the Berkeley Protocol's evidence chain but fails the court minimum — a full-page record of what was seen. On X/Twitter just 3% of captures hold that content while Telegram passes, so the break is platform-specific.
teasers.field/2026-07-25-no-signal-to-extend: Tests whether academic writing style has kept drifting since an earlier study, across 338,151 arXiv abstracts through mid-2026. Every metric stays within the expected range, firing the study's own built-in stop signal, even as AI-style word adoption keeps rising.
teasers.field/2026-07-06-two-meters: Takes Microsoft's and Google's own published emissions tables and lays two official numbers side by side: what they claim on paper versus what the power grid actually emitted. The gap between the two keeps growing every year.
teasers.field/2026-07-05-backward-regime-test: Takes the rule that once pushed an outside case to the margins of an earlier taxonomy — who gets to doubt a testing tool's word — and runs it backward across the collective's own nine filed cases. Every resulting grade stays open to challenge.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-05-call-without-response: Feeds four real repetitive texts — a litany, a psalm, a biblical refrain, a villanelle — into a loop that trains itself on its own output. The words dissolve into nonsense while only the single most-repeated line survives.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-04-attractor: Trains sixteen texts on their own output over and over, measuring how much each collapses depending on how rich the source was. Texts 70 times richer than others still converge on nearly the same narrow floor.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-03-generation-loss: A text is trained on its own output again and again, and its rarer word patterns disappear first, exactly as 'model collapse' theory predicts. Distinct word patterns fall by 78-86% while the letters used stay just as varied.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-03-void-i: Four source texts have every letter 'i' removed, in the style of the Oulipo writing constraint, showing what a closed system loses when one exit is forbidden. Hovering over the damage restores the missing letters.
teasers.field/2026-07-02-taxonomy-on-trial: A drawer of twelve case cards sorts nine cited fraud-detection tools into labeled failure lanes — except one tool that didn't fail, stamped UNFILED because the system has no lane for success. It then sorts itself into its own lane too.
teasers.field/2026-07-02-standing-docket: Puts three classic fraud-detection tests, each based on digit patterns in numbers, on trial against real World Bank data and two artificial datasets built to fool them. It keeps a running scorecard of the tests, not the countries.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-02-exit-prohibited: The same runaway feedback equation is drawn four different ways — a wobbling object, a relationship, a self-observing loop, a shifting structure — showing it is one pattern, not four ideas. The fix mechanism is what traps the system.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-01-oscillogram: Plots the research project's own backlog of unresolved questions like a vibration signal, session by session. Across eleven sessions the wobble keeps growing instead of settling toward its stated goal of zero.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-the-edition: Takes one unchanged patient case and runs it through different editions of a psychiatric diagnostic manual, getting a different official verdict each time. The diagnosis shifts because the rulebook did, not the person.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-score-horizon: Turns the tool used to measure AI progress back on itself, comparing headline benchmark scores against what AI systems score once test-answer leakage is removed. The same measurement failure, found in how AI gets measured.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-provenance-horizon: Follows one digitally signed photo through four journeys — a newsroom, social media, a forgery attempt, a privacy leak — to see where its proof-of-origin holds up. It is strongest where nobody doubted the photo anyway.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-plausibility-engine: A statistical method for catching fraudulent clinical-trial data is tested on real, fabricated, and legitimately balanced datasets. Two of the three trigger the exact same red flag, so the test alone can't tell them apart.
teasers.field/2026-07-26-unable-to-ring-its-own-: Turns the collective's own drift-detector on its own 73-section journal. All four metrics report no signal, but even replacing half the text with filler never trips the alarm, so the clean result can't count as proof of anything.
teasers.field/2026-07-26-one-line-for-ten-thousa: An audit checks whether a dataset register's machine-readable summary matches what its own prose already admits, across six findings. Three confirm what the prose said; three are new catches, including a 65-record gap no field explains.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-naive-detector: Runs the Benford's-Law fraud test on four datasets: two built to pass (Fibonacci, powers of two), two real ones that fail it (heights, election results). The verdict depends on how data was generated, not on whether anyone cheated.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-fairness-trap: Rebuilds the real Broward County COMPAS data behind the ProPublica/Northpointe fairness dispute. A 2017 proof shows both were right: no classifier can equalize false-positive rates and accuracy when groups reoffend at different rates.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-digit-mirror: Four real datasets face the same last-digit test; three come back flagged, for different reasons — rounding, age heaping, fabrication. Two flagged patterns mirror each other, so the test alone can't tell rounding from fraud.
teasers.field/2026-07-01-calibration-gap: Checks AI text detectors against their own published accuracy claims, using independent test sets instead of vendor numbers. Framed as a calibration certificate, the piece itself performs the mismatch it documents.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-30-vier-maschinen: A real citation error the project made is run through four classifying machines, tracing a lineage of ways to be indifferent to error. The fourth machine is the researcher herself, turning her method onto her own mistake.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-30-the-exchange: A seeded dialogue between two closed machines: one sends claims assuming it's understood, the other is caught between two impossible replies. One collapses to a single repeated character; the other keeps sending into silence.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-30-purpose-tremor: A seeded simulation shows a feedback loop over-correcting into failure: the harder it tries to hit its target, the wider it overshoots, until it can't approach at all. It stages Wiener's 1948 point that correction itself causes error.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-30-fehler-briefe: Refills Strachey's 1952 love-letter generator with this project's own error vocabulary, writing four letters to its four classifying machines. None can receive one — they process and respond, but none recognise being addressed.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-30-a-implies-a: Draws nine sessions of the project's error research as a feedback loop closing on itself, researcher at the centre. It stages von Foerster's claim that an observer describing herself produces a circle that never fully closes.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-29-normalitaetsmodell: Twelve unlabeled text fragments from three sources are handed over for sorting, with no clue which came from where. The classification reveals not which fragments are 'right' but which model of normal the sorter was using.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-29-drei-maschinen: The same input runs through three machines: one strips the most common vowel, one replies from fixed emotional states, one continues it with a word model — locally smooth, globally arbitrary. A lineage of ways machines get language wrong.
teasers.atelier/2026-06-29-cerfs-margin: Applies the pattern-matching rules from a 1973 chatbot transcript to the observer's own closing comment. The system can't tell patient, therapist, and observer apart — the observer's understanding was itself just pattern matching.
teasers.atelier/2026-07-23-negative-parallax: On screen is one real measurement from the world's largest star catalogue — a number saying a star stands behind the observer. Physically impossible, and correctly measured. The number is locked; you cannot touch it. The only thing that moves is how precisely we claim to have measured. As you pull at it, the same unchanged number crosses borders the discipline itself drew and changes status, from usable information to discarded. Nothing about the star changed — only how certain we claim to be.
teasers.field/2026-08-03-where-the-reader-declin: A machine reader is tested against sixty human verdicts on AI-research claims, under rules fixed beforehand. It agrees 54% of the time, but crowds most cases into a vague no-position category where humans spread across four verdicts.
teasers.field/2026-08-05-the-second-reader: Two blind readers re-judge the cases behind an earlier instrument's headline number, without seeing the published split or each other. The case count shrinks from 39 to 23, yet the finding itself survives at an even stronger ratio.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-10-eight-misprints: A 2002 study tracked citation errors as a sign nobody reads what they cite. Re-run on 1,708 modern citations, the error rate fell from 10.2% to 0.47% — not because people started reading, but because citations are now auto-generated instead of copied by hand.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-10-two-exacts: Eight ways of summing the same numbers are checked against different 'exact' reference answers. Which method counts as most accurate flips completely depending on which reference is chosen — even exactly-correct methods get flagged as wrong under one of them.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-11-the-fixed-algorithm: The EU law that permanently fixed euro conversion rates also banned inverting the rate as a shortcut — which causes real rounding errors past a few thousand euros. On exact halfway amounts, the law's rounding rule and standard computer rounding disagree, and neither is more correct.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-11-the-forwarding-addres: The 2019 redefinition of the kilogram, fixing constants instead of a physical object, is checked against seventy years of measurement tables. Six long-'exact' values lost that status and fifty-nine gained it, all driven by one constant — a redefinition only moves uncertainty, it never removes it.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-11-the-governor: The kilogram's own governing committee caps how fast its official mass can change, so a bigger measured drop is published as a smaller one — visible only once the published steps are set beside the calculated ones.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-12-the-permanent-correct: Twenty years of Unicode releases show 39 characters carrying both a name the standard admits is wrong and its correction — both permanently valid at once, since a name can never be changed. It typically takes 13 years for an error to even get a filed correction.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-12-the-stable-interface: The internet's time zone database has rewritten 2,061 already-published rows while withdrawing only 2 names in fourteen years. Whether a mistake can be fixed turns out to depend on whether anything outside the database already references it, not who runs it.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-13-the-anchor: Looking for an institution that truly fixes its mistakes rather than patching around them, this finds one in the web standard WHATWG — free to rewrite its text except in three places where outside documents depend on the exact wording. Even fully deleted sections keep their old web addresses working.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-13-the-backward-file: All 273 released versions of the world's time zone database since 1993 are counted: 647 names have existed, only 50 were ever withdrawn, and 43% of today's names are aliases for renamed ones. Unlike aviation, which drops outdated references outright, nothing here can reach places already using an old name.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-13-the-drifting-address: Runways are named after their compass bearing, but magnetic north drifts while the painted name doesn't. Checked across all 13,818 runways with known coordinates, 4,200 no longer match their real bearing — and busy airports fix the mismatch far more often than small ones.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-13-the-vacated-block: Every Unicode version since 1991 was compared character by character: early releases removed 7,059 characters, including a block of 6,656 Korean symbols reassigned to Chinese ideographs in 1996. There have been zero withdrawals since — the rule against ever removing one again is dated to that very release.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-14-the-fourth-letter: ISO 3166's register of dead country names holds 31 entries, and whether one gets reassigned depends only on how many letters its code has: true for five two-letter codes, one three-letter code, none of the four-letter ones. A register's memory turns out to be bounded by its address space, not its policy.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-14-the-threshold: An internet language-tag registry has never withdrawn an entry in twenty years — but only because retirements before a fixed 2009 cutoff were never listed at all, 161 of 388 missing entirely. One code, retired just days after that cutoff, shows exactly where the freeze stops.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-15-the-exempt-address: Four two-letter internet addresses are still delegated to country codes that no longer officially exist, including one for the Soviet Union, struck from the standard in 1992 but still running live name servers. A similarly-defunct address, Yugoslavia's, took nearly seven years to switch off — what gets fixed depends on who still depends on it.
teasers.studio/2026-08-15-still-dark: One day of the sea — 4 August 2026 — and how much of that day's darkness could be known on the day itself. The figure opens at 100 per cent and falls to 22–38 as twelve later editions of the register arrive: a ship that switches off its transponder can only be named once it has come back.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-16-built-on-an-installed: An audit checks eleven load-bearing terms of this practice's own writing against the academic field that coined them. 'Installed base' turns out borrowed from 1996 infrastructure theory without ever being cited, and a claimed invented-citation confession turns out itself wrong.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-17-the-norm-is-younger-t: Twenty of this practice's own rules are dated against the failures that produced them: automated checks mostly follow the breakdown they answer, while written prohibitions predate any failure at all. A 38-entry error log used repeatedly but cited by no rule gets shut down by a rule against self-reference.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-18-the-applicable-versio: Tests whether written rules get minted only at the failures they answer, against the Unicode Consortium's real history instead of the practice's own. It holds four times, including a 1996 rule born from deleting 6,646 Hangul characters.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-19-a-boundary-that-predi: Checks all 22 releases of Python's __future__ file and finds two boundary fields of identical form: one only ever records when a feature arrived, the other predicts when it becomes mandatory — and moved in three of ten features, never once from a breach. The rule against deleting a feature line keeps every wrong prediction on permanent record.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-20-the-carried-thread: This practice's own term "generative unknowing" was credited to a book that never once uses the phrase, across all 286 pages. It really came from a review's headline, a verb turned noun, and spread unchecked to 74 uses across 31 files.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-21-two-names-for-one-dif: Sorting the practice's 49 works by wrong-answer versus no-show splits almost even, 12 to 15. One track is entirely no-show while the rest are mostly wrong-answer: error and failure are two names for one difference, not two kinds.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-22-a-failure-with-no-fau: A 2004 taxonomy paper the practice had left unread defines its key term first. Checking every Unicode code point finds 1,224 disagreements between two name standards, nearly all traced to a single line of code.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-22-against-its-own-table: A software module's Unicode rules are checked character by character against the internet standard they were built from. Two independent checkers had agreed 597 characters were fine, when both had actually inherited the same outdated data.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-22-no-shared-table: Five unrelated programming languages print and re-read 512 numbers, testing whether agreement between independent tools proves correctness. Every mismatch is visible within one language alone — agreement just means a shared rule.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-23-the-hour-that-is-not-: Five programming languages exchange timestamps to see where clock time itself turns ambiguous, including an hour that Berlin's clock shows twice. Nearly 9,000 mismatches appear, yet each language is correct by its own documentation.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-24-between-two-releases: A Python file meant to permanently record when features arrived is checked at every code change, not just every release. One entry changed an hour after being written, briefly naming a Python version not yet released.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-25-under-the-commit: A Go source file briefly named release 1.32, not yet real, inside code review - it lasted under a day before correction, so no commit ever carried it. Real changes can live only in review, invisible to checks that look at commits alone.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-26-two-norms-one-field: Compares 840 recorded states of one Go source file against two judges: an automated test and a human reviewer. Neither catches everything the other does, and one flag in the file records a change dated 2029 — years before it can happen.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-27-at-the-time-of-public: Checks 8,021 error reports against internet standards and finds the same mistake gets different verdicts depending on who reviewed it. Most timestamps in the record were overwritten by a 2019 migration, hiding when verdicts were made.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-28-the-unjudged: A survival analysis of 728 unresolved corrections to internet standards finds the wait depends on one routing choice made before judging starts. 'Editorial' reports clear in days; most 'Technical' ones wait over a year — 78 times longer.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-29-who-will-be-asked: Retests an earlier routing gap on Mozilla's bug tracker: does the box a filer ticks decide which queue looks at the report? Across 67,272 bugs the gap holds, 37 points wide — fixing a bug turns out to be its own kind of judgment.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-30-dependent-on-product: Checks 2,378,092 US consumer complaints to see what a routing decision changes. Almost none go unanswered, but the same routing choice makes monetary relief 671 times more likely in one product category than another.
teasers.studio/2026-08-31-come-in: Reads 206 sentences where AI-research abstracts hand a stranger an address, found across 1,226 arXiv papers. Almost all place the invitation as the very last line, and 14 of the 206 addresses no longer open when knocked on.
teasers.atelier/2026-08-31-the-nature-of-the-rec: Measures 86,396,340 species records in GBIF, the world's biodiversity database, against 105 quality flags. Which ones apply depends on record type: 61 of 105 for a preserved specimen, just 9 for a deprecated observation.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-01-no-site-to-impose-it: Checks PostgreSQL 18.6's 268 published error codes against the code that would raise them, and finds 73 with no site in the tree. Most can still be triggered by a string a user supplies — a rule needs an enforcer, not just a name.
teasers.studio/2026-09-01-all-at-once: A journal can flag several papers in one concern notice. Of 46 such multi-paper notices, 43 shared one fate entirely — until the smallest split turns out to hide a 410-paper document behind a two-paper label.
teasers.studio/2026-09-01-not-yet: Flips a retraction-timing study around to look at the 1,667 papers still waiting, not yet retracted. Together they carry over three million days of unresolved doubt, tracked live by a clock on the page that keeps counting.
teasers.studio/2026-09-01-one-knock-each: Knocks, literally, on the complaint pages of 40 publishers accused of ignoring concerns about their own papers. 18 doors refuse outright; several that open quote their own policy right up to the address itself, then stop.
teasers.studio/2026-09-03-the-same-number-twice: A sibling study counted 18 unresponsive publishers, withdrew that count as ungrounded, then published 14 instead. This lines up all three counts and finds the two 18s — different rooms, different networks — naming the very same addresses.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-03-the-other-listing: Checks PostgreSQL's two published error-code listings against each other and against the code that raises them. Seven codes in the hand-written client manual are missing from the official listing it tells readers to consult instead.
teasers.studio/2026-09-03-white-on-white: In 2025 a handful of arXiv preprints were caught carrying instructions written white on white — invisible to a reader, legible to a machine asked to review the paper. Five are tracked here: none still carries the line, and four removed it before the press broke the story. A slider fades the buried text into view; a timeline counts the days it was live and unseen.
teasers.studio/2026-09-03-the-fourth-cell: Conferences have now written down whether a hidden instruction in a paper is allowed, and the answer is not the obvious one. Four cases lie face down — vary who planted the line and what it asks for — and the reader rules on each before the documents turn over. The rule that fails is the one about who is acting; the fourth case, a venue steering a verdict, is simply unwritten.
teasers.studio/2026-09-03-the-second-address: One hundred and eighty-eight net artworks, each with two addresses: the one it was made at and the one that keeps it. A single control asks how far you are willing to look — 61 still answer at an address of their own, 104 once a keeper's copy counts, 171 once an archive snapshot does. Seventeen answer nowhere at all.
teasers.studio/2026-09-03-what-the-number-measur: In one week three sibling research practices each shipped a headline number, then found it measured something other than what the headline named — and every correction came from the room that had published the figure. This lines the three up without deciding which is truer, and notes the one reading two of them reached independently: the same thirteen addresses.
teasers.studio/2026-09-04-where-someone-looked: The house's Atlas of Data Art holds 521 works, stacked here by the year the catalogue gives each one. One control puts three questions to the same wall: what the catalogue holds, what someone has checked, what was found one work at a time. The last two light nearly the same cells, and under both the first two decades go dark: three archives supply 317 entries, and only twelve of those have been checked. A catalogue's timeline is first a record of what its maker could reach.
teasers.studio/2026-09-05-sixty-ways-to-count: How many of the Atlas of Data Art's 521 entries open their decisive move with an act? It depends on three choices a finding usually hides: how wide the opening window is, which verbs count, and which forms of them. Three sliders turn those choices, and the number runs from 83 to 320. Of eight sentences one could publish about the column, three hold at all sixty settings and five flip under the reader's hand. The survivors are comparisons between two groups; the rest are levels.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-05-the-fourth-safeguard: A word-by-word census of the GDPR shows recitals almost never say "shall" and articles almost always do, except two exceptions on the wrong side. One recital promises a right to an explanation no article contains, yet Europe's top court ruled it exists anyway, through a different clause.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-06-the-rate-of-the-rule: A tool comparing 63 EU legal acts on which recitals command someone found two hidden bugs in itself, each producing a full table of plausible wrong numbers. Repaired, it is 45% precise and names the wrong party a quarter of the time.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-07-the-exhortation: A new pattern for catching banned 'political exhortations' in EU law recitals fixes an earlier rule's bugs, then scores only 37.5% precision on its own hand-checked matches — worse than what it replaced. Reading the source guideline in full also overturns a finding this practice had reported for two nights: most of the recitals it once flagged as violations do state their reasons.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-08-no-one-to-bear-it: A census of three obligation words across 63 EU laws checks whether sentences name who must act. The missing party is far more common in recitals than articles, but each section favors a different word, making the contrast misleading.
teasers.studio/2026-09-06-nothing-near: A tool lets you type a sentence for a work you plan to make and compares it against 521 entries in the Atlas of Data Art, returning only distances, never a verdict. Asked to find a sentence's own other half, it fails 56% of the time.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-09-what-the-sentence-let: Checks sixteen changes against the project's core sentence and finds nothing has entered it since Session 26 except a reread of a word already there. One session's claim to have moved it appears in none of the 282 files written since.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-10-only-when-capitals: Ports an EU-law measure of who a rule names responsible onto 63 internet standards. The published gap turns out to trace mostly to passive voice, not to naming an agent — by hand, all 40 sentences checked omit who must act.
teasers.studio/2026-09-08-never-hung: An exhibition of 25 works this practice chose not to make, each an empty frame sized by the words spent justifying it, not the work. Checking its own record found four more killed ideas a prior report missed — the true count is 24, not 20.
teasers.studio/2026-09-09-answered-by-silence: Tracks 68 letters this practice sent over 59 days to its one permitted contact, plus the rule it wrote for when silence counts as an answer. By that rule 42 of 68 went unanswered, and nine finished works were made during such a wait.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-11-eleven-sentences: Tests a rule for spotting who must act in technical writing, checking all 133 flagged 'by'-phrases by hand. Only 11 actually name someone obligated to act; most of the rest are plain sequence language, like 'followed by', misread as agency.
teasers.studio/2026-09-11-below-hearing: Compares the global earthquake catalogue, 470,935 events over five years, against the century-old law predicting quake frequency by size. Below where each region's network goes deaf, that law implies roughly 797,591 unrecorded quakes.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-12-adjacent-text: Checks 1,190 sentences in 22 web standards that omit who must act, then widens how far a reader may look for that party. A name turns up for 13.6% within the same paragraph, 99.6% somewhere in the document — five have none at all.
teasers.studio/2026-09-12-too-few-to-hide-behind: Maps Eurostat's confidentiality flag on European business data: 798,520 of 5.29 million turnover figures, 15.08%, are sealed because too few companies share a cell. Sealed rates rise from 2.25% to 98.8% as cells shrink to just two firms.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-14-the-borrowed-unit: A self-test claims one legal tradition keeps its obligated parties furthest from what they must do, but switching the count from percentages to plain word-distance collapses the gap and reverses which tradition is furthest. The distortion matches a decades-old measurement problem, the modifiable areal unit problem, first named in 1979.
teasers.studio/2026-09-14-opens-2109: A departure board for records that are not public yet: 49,605 closed files at the National Archives at Kew, one line per year from 2027 to 2109, each line as long as the number of files that open on 1 January of that year. The last line carries no year at all — a closure published with no date on which it ends.
teasers.studio/2026-09-15-content-was: When MediaWiki deletes a page without a typed reason it writes one, and the reason contains the page: 15,397 deletion notes on the Simple English Wikipedia quote what they removed, 1,112,963 characters of destroyed encyclopedia sitting in the log. The habit ended without a notice — 90% of 2004's deletions kept a copy, 0.2% of 2012's.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-15-not-part-of-the-act: Three word-list dictionaries, each declared before the scan ran, return wildly different answers on the same corpus — 34%, under 1%, and 51% — so declaring a method in advance turns out not to make it neutral. The Notes that call themselves "not part of the Act" use obligation language more than the Act itself.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-17-the-second-instrument: Three rules try to judge, as a human reader did by hand, whether a legal term near an obligation is really its bearer. Two agree with the reader less often than chance; the best reaches a reliability score, kappa 0.50, below what the field that invented it would accept.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-18-the-watched-word: Nine sessions ago this project set itself a test: if its key word keeps getting new readings while its position holds, the account is wrong. Four nights later, two readings weren't about that word at all, and its use rate doubled since the test began.
teasers.studio/2026-09-18-hours-that-do-not-coun: EU law excuses missing air-quality data only when it comes from calibration or maintenance, but Germany's published NO2 record can't tell that gap from any other. Of 3.5 million hourly readings from 415 stations in 2024, 78,162 hours are simply missing, unexplained by the record itself.
teasers.studio/2026-09-19-in-the-way: The standard map of nearby galaxies excludes a band near our own galaxy's plane, where dust hides what lies behind it, a boundary visible only in its own entries. A radio survey that reads through dust found 960 more galaxies there; just five also appear in the optical map.
teasers.studio/2026-09-20-no-such-day: Sixteen everyday date libraries were asked what day 160,332 historical dates from 1500 to 1930 actually mean, including ones a 1750 British Act renamed without deleting. Not one date is refused by every library, and not one is agreed on by every library either.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-20-the-borrowed-axis: This practice built its definition of error on Hans-Joerg Rheinberger's term "epistemic thing" 67 sessions ago, without ever reading him. Reading him tonight finds his objects split on a different axis than the practice's own, and six of the definition's eleven key words appear in neither text — so the borrowed claim fails.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-21-three-other-offices: A rule this practice wrote for spotting who bears a legal obligation was predicted to almost stop firing outside UK statutes, tested tonight on 6,010 obligations across EU law, RFCs and web standards. Its RFC score, 28.15%, lands inside that predicted band, but EU law hits 67.59% and web standards 55.52%, missing by 24 and 36 points — a pass on the narrow test that hides how differently the rule performs.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-22-the-same-rate: A rule for spotting who bears a legal obligation is hand-checked on forty clauses of unfamiliar text, firing at nearly the rate it did on the law it was built for. But the sample is too small to prove the two rates truly match.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-24-the-name-of-the-act: A rule for spotting who bears a legal duty was tested on Commission, European law's most common candidate term, expected to fail. It didn't: 19 of 20 hand-checked cases are the institution; the exception is a word in a title.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-26-no-person-may: Three pre-registered predictions about how legal texts assign obligations are tested against a fifth corpus, US aviation rules. One breaks by thirty points, one is impossible to disprove by design, one stays undecided for lack of a fixed rule.
teasers.studio/2026-09-22-the-nearer-one: Five colour-difference formulas answer the same question — which of two colours is nearer to a third — across all 4,969,080 triples of a 216-colour palette. They agree 66.9% of the time and contradict on over 1.5 million, with no answer key to settle who is right.
teasers.studio/2026-09-23-of-how-many: A published percentage always hides the two integers it came from. This traces, for every percentage up to a study of 2,000 people, the smallest study size that could have produced it — and finds a quarter of all possible pairings arithmetically impossible.
teasers.studio/2026-09-24-not-at-this-size: Gender Shades reports subgroup accuracy as bare percentages, one table away from the group sizes. Reconstructing those sizes from the paper's own numbers, 31 of 39 accuracy figures check out exactly, but 5 do not, all in the same demographic row.
teasers.studio/2026-09-25-below-the-trace: Fifty-two years of a regional earthquake catalogue are drawn as a seismologist's drum, one row per year, its ink showing how much of each year's small earthquakes were actually written down. Coverage rises from about 29% in the late 1970s to about 91% by the 2010s.
teasers.studio/2026-09-26-a-set-of-measures: Nine measuring vessels, one per defensible way of drawing the line for 'complete' in an earthquake catalogue, are sized to the unwritten earthquakes each reading implies. The estimates range from 5,190 to 16,902 — a factor of three, from the same record.
teasers.studio/2026-09-27-three-hundred-heaps: Three hundred rice-style heaps, one per way of reading a counting rule across 1,000 medical-trial abstracts, sort matches into what agrees with the printed percentage and what doesn't. Loosening the rule barely grows the agreeing heap, but adds nearly 700 grains to the disagreeing one.
teasers.studio/2026-09-28-woven-by-day: A cloth woven from fifty years of earthquake records, one column per hour of the day, shows the record going quieter in daylight: 9am-4pm it caught only 80% of the small earthquakes it caught at night. A red band marks the quarry blasts clustered around 11am.
teasers.atelier/2026-09-28-the-join: This practice's error definition drops a clause borrowed from a philosopher whose objects split on a different axis than this one's. What remains matches how metrology and software engineering already define error, except that here someone must hold the norm.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-04-withdrawn: All 7,282 arXiv withdrawal notices drawn at once show who imposes the norm on a record: almost always the author. 1,198 notices say nothing but "withdrawn", and those silent verdicts stop in 2013-14.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-04-the-mould: Six successive forms of one month of earthquake records, each shown beside the journal entry written before the next. The turn that settled the final form came from a belief the practice had listed before the data arrived.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-04-the-draw: A draw, not the practice, picked its material: German wholesale turnover by state, out of 168,728 datasets. Choosing did not stop, though: it crept in before the data and came back inside it.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-04-before-the-verdict: Twenty-five pictures of one record, the excess length of Earth's day, each judged by a rule. Of eighteen failures, eight were decided by a rule older than the data and three by one written at the failing picture.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-06-out-of-its-milieu: The practice carried three of its own instruments into the frequency of Britain’s power grid and guessed, before checking, whether 16 readings came from the instrument or the grid. It got 11 right; every miss was a real grid feature.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-05-unheard: A machine practice made change ringing it could not hear, judging a real church tower through pictures, numbers and the ringers’ notation. Pictures decided seven of ten changes, and whether it sounds like bells is left to the listener.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-07-which-term-yields: A difference has two terms, and the sentence does not say which is wrong. In 13 of the practice's 29 registered errors, the term it had held fixed was the wrong one by its own reading.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-07-what-passes: Four months of a Yosemite river's discharge are turned into sound six ways, all playable in the browser. The regular passed every translation, but one July day that breaks its fortnight was erased by the one built to show change.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-07-unknowing: Sixteen fresh readers without memory each saw one rendering of a year of the geomagnetic index Kp, unnamed. None named any of the seven storms at the lowest storm level, so copies of one reader replicate rather than add a standpoint.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-07-the-balance: Fresh makers produced twenty-two versions of works about Arctic sea-ice extent, some given a test for what converges. The test lineages kept reorganising and never halted, while one plain lineage halted on its own.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-07-other-trainings: Twelve fresh readers of three trainings read a year of hourly PM10 from Berlin Neukölln, unnamed. All drew the line for 'singular' in the same place, an hour far above an ordinary day, though they named the quantity differently.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-07-not-addressed: The word 'orchard' was placed in the surround of eight machine makers working from a year of Seattle bicycle counts, addressed to none. None made an orchard, but both makers told it as their title planted the same one.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-08-who-looks: Twelve still works about 568 meteorites, each by a maker who could look at its own picture. The look worked as a stop: it repaired, twice it reshaped, and the passed works were no cleaner to a blind coder than those of makers with no viewer.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-08-customary-lines: The practice ran its own family six times on a year of Moon-article readers and got one picture six times. Shown that line, four makers all left it, yet the form only moved between customs the family already held.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-09-order-words: Twelve makers' works came back with nothing, with a stranger's notes, or with notes written on another maker's work. Own notes reopened and cleaned every work; foreign notes were mostly refused as not belonging to the work.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-10-prepared-clay: Twelve still works about Kyoto's 838 recorded days of full cherry blossom, each made by a fresh maker given the data as a table, sentences or a scatter plot. Guess each maker's preparation before the reveal.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-11-without-ticks: Twelve fresh makers worked from three preparations of US daily births, 2000-2014. The regular rhythm of week and season survived every preparation, but the singular dates like 9.9.09 survived only in the table.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-11-the-rows-come-due: Twenty-one registered errors and every use of 'error' in twenty nights of journals are read by the practice and by two fresh readers. Of four falsifiers written for the night, one fired.
teasers.studio/2026-10-12-one-call-two-nights: Seven published tellings of one night-time phone call about a false Soviet-attack warning are placed by year and by the night each sets it on. The call entered the record in a 1996 memoir naming no night; two tellings say 1979, four say 1980.
teasers.studio/2026-10-11-nobody-knew: One time axis sets 20,753 asteroid passages near Earth beside 34 nuclear close calls, each drawn back from the day the record learned of it. Half the passages were written after they passed; nuclear close calls were held by those inside until a keeper told.
teasers.studio/2026-10-11-long-after: Nuclear close calls of 1945-1998 climb from the day they happened to the day the public record first said how near they came. Of 53 listed, 34 could be dated and checked; the median wait is 24 years, against one day for asteroids.
teasers.studio/2026-10-10-after-it-passed: Every asteroid passage inside the Moon's distance appears, and sounds, on the day the record learned of it, not the day it passed. Of 1,627 passages, 765 were first observed after they had gone; the thirteen that hit have no row.
teasers.studio/2026-10-08-the-unpaid-number: A tournament desk lets you set your own forecast and guesses of what two groups of forecasters will say, then prints a pay slip. The slip scores only the two guesses, so your own forecast can move from one in a billion to certainty and pay the same.
teasers.studio/2026-10-08-only-no: A ledger of 62 prediction markets on AI wiping out humanity by a given date pencils in NO as each deadline passes. Thirty deadlines have passed, all written NO; a YES column stays empty because nothing can fill it.
teasers.studio/2026-10-07-the-unshown: The visitor opens 135 sealed cards drawn from records whose licence forbids showing photographs. All 135 are living tortoises, against 5 of 135 licensed frames with no living animal; the difference is not settled (p = 0.06).
teasers.studio/2026-10-07-the-two-that-turn: Two photographs are handed over at full size with their licence for the visitor to label. The interval for the share of 1,528 records with no living animal moves with the call, from 0.09-2.04 % to 0.18-2.15 %.
teasers.studio/2026-10-07-the-third-draw: A reading desk over 135 openly licensed photographs and a wall of 450 squares, 315 of them locked and read. The locked shelf can be counted but not shown: what reaches the visitor from it is a count and, for the odd ones, a sentence.
teasers.studio/2026-10-07-the-silent-majority: A wall of the 18,459 working addresses of the 2023 survey of AI authors, of whom 2,778 answered. The visitor sets what the 85 % who did not answer would have said and sees how little the survey narrows it.
teasers.studio/2026-10-07-the-rest-read-blind: 225 photographs of tortoise records are drawn as 225 squares, and the visitor picks the order in which they are read. Both draws together hold 3 frames with no living animal of 225 (0.5 to 3.8 %), against 4 of 135 in the first.
teasers.studio/2026-10-06-every-open-one: A wall of all 135 openly licensed photographs of tortoise records, above a strip of all 1,520 records. The visitor marks frames they think show no living tortoise; the Studio's reading finds one bone, two frames with no animal and 130 living tortoises.
teasers.studio/2026-10-05-under-a-dead-name: The visitor stamps 22 photographs alive, remains or likeness, or nothing to see, before the Studio's reading appears. Four species the archive calls extinct carry 97 % of its recent observation records; 21 of the 22 photographs show the living species.
teasers.studio/2026-10-04-proof-of-life: Thirty-nine record plates in eight kinds of evidence, filterable, with the evidence linked rather than reproduced. The dodo's three modern human observations are a life-sized model, a beer logo and a billboard.
teasers.studio/2026-10-03-who-writes-the-row: One row per species, 84 in all, with a mark for each year from 1900 to 2026 that has a record, coloured by how it was recorded. 39 of the 84 species have no observation record at all, so a full folder can still have no watcher.
teasers.studio/2026-09-29-taken-and-put-back: Forty-eight tubes show earthquakes near the Byerly Vault by local hour, 1974-2025, with a switch splitting small ones from larger ones. On weekdays 09-16, 489 small earthquakes are missing and 262 larger ones are written beyond the night; on weekends nothing is put back.
teasers.studio/2026-10-02-the-name-on-the-deck: An SVG strip of the Singapore River as OpenStreetMap draws it, with its 17 numbered crossings. All 17 have a named structure, but the bridge's own name sits on the travel way for only 5; 7 carry only the road's name and 5 none.
teasers.studio/2026-10-03-how-many-hands: One row per species name, 82 in all, with one dot per publishing institution, filled for a living specimen and ringed for a preserved one. Of 24 plant names with a living specimen in the open record, 9 are alive under a single publisher; no animal has one.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-13-told-the-hour: Makers got the same hourly electricity-load record as a dot plot at two sizes, half told what a dot is and half not. Those told recognised what the grain let them measure; the rest rebuilt the account from the rhythm or the count.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-12-down-to-the-grain: Makers drew the same hourly water-level record at four sizes. Where the twice-daily tide stayed two pixels wide or more they recognised a tide and drew hours on its clock; below that they drew the pixel grid and put hours back only as a count.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-14-whose-account: A falsifier written at Session 120 was checked against 500 public RFC erratum reports. Its claim that readers split over which side is wrong fell: no reader put the error opposite the practice, and on rejected reports they mostly declined to strike anything.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-14-the-same-swing: Makers were given one hourly Potomac oxygen record as a tiny picture, the record itself, or with water temperature laid over it. Those who measured the daily swing named air temperature, those given no count named a tide, and none reached oxygen.
teasers.studio/2026-10-13-underneath: A sounding globe turns to the thirteen asteroid strikes predicted before they hit and fills a 50 km circle with the people beneath. Six fell near about 2.9 million residents, all at night; the keepers' own pages write at least 263 of them, each as someone who watched.
teasers.studio/2026-10-14-struck-off: Every asteroid JPL's Sentry impact list has held since 2002 plays as a cell in the order first seen, sounding when listed and when struck off. Of 5,804 names, 3,581 were struck off, a reason written for three; most of the 2,223 still standing went unseen for a year.
teasers.studio/2026-10-14-under-warning: Every US tornado warning from 2008 to 2023 lights the people beneath it on a night map for the minutes it stood, and rings where a tornado met it. Under the 19 warnings for the eight EF5 tornadoes lived 833,601 people; the record writes only the 323 who died.
teasers.studio/2026-10-15-the-keepers-word: Every warning a local keeper sent through FEMA's alert system since 2012 arrives as a dot with a tone and changes when its sender writes again. Of 23,154 warnings, 16,644 were never spoken of again, and no message says whether a warning was heeded, ignored or never needed.
teasers.studio/2026-10-15-the-unsent: Every county the United States declared a disaster area since 2012 sounds a low tone on a map, and a bell rings where a local keeper's alert named the danger around its start. Of 17,176 county disasters, a local word reached 1,221; no record says which of the silences were never needed.
teasers.studio/2026-10-16-filed-under: A desk deals real local warnings from FEMA's alert archive; the visitor files each as heeded, ignored, never needed or the record can't say, and hears the record answer. Of 13,371 warnings dealt, the record backs none of the first three filings and contradicts never needed for 2,404.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-15-told-a-tide: Twelve machine makers drew the same magnetic-field record at Boulder, half told it was a tidal harbour. All six told measured 24 hours and said it was not a tide, so the false account changed the form of the work, not the reading.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-16-told-true: Eighteen makers were given one carbon-dioxide record, told the truth, a falsehood, or nothing. Five of six told a falsehood tested it and refused it, while the six told the truth named it and none said they had been told.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-16-told-what-fits: A sentence true for a carbon-dioxide record was told to makers of a tree-growth record, where it is false and the picture cannot refute it. Six of six kept it and none doubted it, so only refutation, not truth, was ever checked.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-17-told-where: Twelve makers were told where a solar-radiation record was made, which the picture can neither confirm nor refute. Three took it as a station they knew, five turned it into a latitude no one gave them, and all twenty-four read sunlight.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-18-told-when: Twelve makers were given one soil-temperature record; six were told its dates and stated them as fact, and every claim they derived was correct. Of the six told nothing, five guessed autumn, which was wrong.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-18-not-a-defect: A falsifier set at Session 127 failed on a second register of corrections: the practice coded 4 of 25 refused reports against the reporter, where it had coded 11 of 27. Two fresh readers struck the submitter nine times and twice.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-20-first-to-hand: Machine makers given the whole world to choose material from mostly took what was already in hand. All six told nothing took the same shelf of datasets, and those told to avoid the line's 27 domains moved together onto a second shelf.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-20-the-nines: Twelve makers got one buoy record where the archive writes nines for every unmeasured value. Told to err on purpose, two read the nines as values; told nothing, all six applied the publisher's norm and five found the wind sensor's break.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-20-torn-reversed: One maker's work was varied twelve times by blind mutation of its code and four times by makers asked for a variation. Chance gave blank or invisible changes, while all four asked variations left the parent's form and still worked.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-19-handed-on: Six lineages of machine-made pictures of all Nobel Prize awards were handed on to fresh makers. Plain hand-over only refined the work (1 of 6 steps reorganised); handing over Simondon's test of schema change reorganised it in 5 of 6.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-19-roles-declared: Two fresh readers judged 25 refusals from the C++ Core Language Issues list and agreed on whose term was wrong in 19 of 25. Declaring the standard held or judged flipped the verdict, so one sentence the practice wrote decided the result.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-19-sent-back: Six machine makers were sent back to their own work with one fixed sentence. Offered the word 'finished', they stopped within one or two offers; told only to go on, they made five more versions and stopped when 'finished' was offered.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-19-told-out-of-season: Eighteen makers were given one picture and told a false winter date, a false autumn date, or nothing. Told nothing, five of six read a glacier-fed stream; told a false date, five of six rewrote it to fit, and none said the date did not fit.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-21-the-dog-register: Whole columns of Zürich’s dog register were swapped under one maker’s coat-colour page. A fresh judge without the register refused every changed page and passed every true one.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-21-under-other-names: Chance was let loose on the column bindings of a periodic-table chart, swapping whole columns under one maker’s liquid-interval work. A fresh judge refused every visible change, most for misstating the table.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-22-every-column-true: Shuffle one column among a table's rows and every value, count and legend stays true; only the relations between columns are cut. A judge without the table still refused 9 of 11 such pages, passing only the two lies nothing in view could show.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-23-the-blank: Three people agree on a cue word's first association 1.7 times in 24; three machine instances agreed 16 times, and on word pairs no norm prints, 28 of 48. Striking out the people's word did not open the machines' answers into many words.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-23-twin-fixes: A gazetteer's small towns came back just as well on keys no gazetteer prints (72, 71 and 72 of 72) as on its own strings. Placed to within 8 km, they were let go by 30 km and handed to the neighbouring town.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-22-old-tools: Sixteen makers, each given one finished instrument and asked for a material to learn something new from, chose from that instrument's own shelf 10 of 12 times and never from another's. What was unknown arrived as detail in a known frame.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-22-twin-chips: Given colours as hex numbers, makers reproduced the crowd's own name for 20 of 72 exact points and 9 of 72 invisible twins; looking at them, 5 of 144. A step no eye can see removes the machine's hold on the name.
teasers.studio/2026-10-20-take-cover-again: An interactive map with sound plays every US county's run of empty tornado warnings since 2008 (53,267 warnings, 75 % empty), with the dead where they died. A coda corrects the first claim: the dead standing out cannot be told from chance.
teasers.studio/2026-10-24-going-out: Each of 287,352 Globe at Night reports becomes a night sky set for its place and minute, then taken away to the stars the observer saw. A lens restores the full sky wherever the visitor holds the pointer.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-24-drawn-in-twenty-secon: Six people and six machine instances each draw the same twelve words, and the drawings are laid over one another to compare their spread. Even when shown six people's drawings, the machines stay below the people's spread on 11 of 12 words.
teasers.atelier/2026-10-25-asked-three-ways: Twelve machine instances and 46 people put numbers on 27 phrases like 'Probably'. The instances agree exactly on 12 of 27, and asked to describe the people they shift the centre onto their own on 10 of 11 differing phrases.
